thread.title: Warm weather accelerates pest development in Pennsylvania Christmas tree farms
thread.title_full: Warm weather accelerates pest development in Pennsylvania Christmas tree farms

author: Keystone Today
title: Warm weather accelerates pest development in Pennsylvania Christmas tree farms
text:
Christmas tree growers across Pennsylvania are experiencing rapid pest development due to warm and relatively dry conditions, according to a June 10 report from Penn State Extension. Scattered thunderstorms brought variable rainfall, with some farms receiving beneficial moisture while others remained dry. The continued warm temperatures have favored the emergence of scale crawlers and increased spider mite activity.
The report highlights that growing degree day accumulations have advanced quickly in several counties, which correlates with ongoing elongate hemlock scale crawler activity, the start of cryptomeria scale crawler emergence, declining spruce spider mite populations, and the beginning of bagworm hatch on susceptible hosts. Growers are advised to rely on site-specific scouting since pest development can vary significantly between locations.
Elongate hemlock scale remains active in many Fraser fir plantings. The presence of overlapping life stages was observed during recent scouting efforts. “Several growers reported successful applications targeting crawler emergence,” the report states. As more crawlers settle and develop protective coverings, contact insecticides become less effective. Products labeled for crawler suppression include bifenthrin products such as Talstar and Onyx, Safari (dinotefuran), and Movento (spirotetramat). Thorough coverage of needle undersides is emphasized for successful management.
Cryptomeria scale crawler activity is also increasing across parts of Pennsylvania. Eggs, newly emerged crawlers, and settled crawlers may all be present simultaneously as hatch progresses. Management options during this stage include bifenthrin products like Talstar and Onyx, Distance (pyriproxyfen), Centaur (buprofezin), Safari (dinotefuran), among others targeting exposed crawlers.
Other pests mentioned in the report include spruce spider mites—whose populations appear lower than earlier this spring—eriophyid mites at low levels not warranting treatment unless numbers increase substantially; Fletcher scale—which has not yet reached egg hatch—and arborvitae leafminer found on Emerald Green arborvitae trees but currently only causing cosmetic damage.
Growers managing arborvitae should monitor both Fletcher scale development and leafminer activity while tracking growing degree day accumulations toward anticipated crawler emergence later this summer. Bagworms have not yet been reported from Christmas tree scouting locations within Pennsylvania but early instar larvae were observed in neighboring Maryland; several counties now exceed thresholds associated with bagworm egg hatch, so immediate monitoring is recommended for susceptible hosts.
A follow-up on Green Giant arborvitae previously affected by winter injury shows most trees are recovering well after recent fungicide applications; environmental stress remains identified as a primary contributor to previous symptoms rather than disease alone.
General recommendations urge growers to continue close monitoring for pests—especially scales—as temperatures rise through scattered thunderstorms statewide. Regular scouting is called “the most valuable tool for protecting tree quality through the remainder of the growing season.” Applicators are reminded that “the label is the law,” regarding pesticide use compliance under federal and state regulations.
Penn State Extension delivers science-based education throughout every county via local offices and digital tools; it provides workshops, online courses, consultations on farming topics including pest control, and collaborates with government agencies and industry partners for educational programming focused on agriculture, nutrition, community well-being, innovation support, as well as environmental stewardship according to the official website .
summary: Christmas tree growers across Pennsylvania are experiencing rapid pest development due to warm and relatively dry conditions, according to a June 10 report from Penn State Extension. Management options during this stage include bifenthrin products like Talstar and Onyx, Distance (pyriproxyfen), Centaur (buprofezin), Safari (dinotefuran), among others targeting exposed crawlers. Growers managing arborvitae should monitor both Fletcher scale development and leafminer activity while tracking growing degree day accumulations toward anticipated crawler emergence later this summer.
